A Swiss study found that 11 out of 13 thermal printing papers contained 8–17 g/kg of BPA. When dry fingers came into contact with a thermal paper receipt, approximately 1 μg of BPA (ranging from 0.2–6 μg) was transferred to the forefinger and middle finger. For wet or greasy fingers, the amount transferred was approximately ten times higher. While dermal absorption of BPA is not a significant concern, free BPA can easily transfer to the skin, and residues on hands can be ingested. Studies conducted by the CDC found BPA in the urine of 95% of adults sampled between 1988 and 1994, and in 93% of children and adults tested in 2003–2004. A 2009 study demonstrated that drinking from polycarbonate bottles increased urinary BPA levels by two-thirds, from 1.2 to 2 micrograms per gram of creatinine. To minimize the risk of BPA leaching into food or beverages, the National Toxicology Panel advises against microwaving food in plastic containers, placing plastics in the dishwasher, or using harsh detergents. In the U.S., consumption of soda, school lunches, and meals prepared outside the home was statistically associated with higher urinary BPA levels. BPA is also used in the epoxy resin coating of water pipes, particularly in older buildings, to prevent the replacement of deteriorating hot and cold water pipes. Infants fed liquid formula, especially from polycarbonate bottles, can consume up to 13 μg/kg/day of BPA. In the U.S. and Canada, BPA has been detected in infant liquid formula at concentrations ranging from 0.48 to 11 ng/g, though it is rarely found in infant powder formula. While breastfeeding is the optimal source of nutrition for infants, it is not always feasible. The U.S. In the U.S. Pregnant women exposed to BPA can transfer it to their fetuses. Animal studies have shown that BPA can be detected in the placenta and amniotic fluid of pregnant mice. A small U.S. study in 2009 detected an average of 2.8 ng/mL of BPA in the blood of 9 out of 10 umbilical cords tested. A study in Japan tested plastic baby books for potential BPA leaching into saliva when chewed by infants. The pharmacokinetics of BPA in humans remain a topic of debate among scientists. In the liver, BPA undergoes glucuronidation, forming the metabolite BPA-glucuronide (BPAG), which reduces free BPA levels. However, BPAG can be deconjugated by beta-glucuronidase, an enzyme found in high concentrations in the placenta and other tissues. Free BPA can also be inactivated by sulfation, a process reversible by arylsulfatase C. A 2010 in vitro study suggested that placental P-glycoprotein may efflux BPA from the placenta. The best methods for studying BPA effects are still under discussion, with scientists holding differing opinions. A 2010 review of over 80 biomonitoring studies concluded that the general population is internally exposed to significant amounts of unconjugated BPA, typically in the ng/mL blood range. Using GC/MS analysis on 20 samples, BPA was detected in 100% of urine samples (median: 1.25 ng/mL) and 10% of blood samples (LOD: 0.5 ng/mL). A 2009 study found that certain drugs, such as naproxen, salicylic acid, carbamazepine, and mefenamic acid, can significantly inhibit BPA glucuronidation in vitro. Additionally, a 2010 study on rat embryos found that genistein may enhance the developmental toxicity of BPA. Environmental studies have shown that BPA can affect growth, reproduction, and development in aquatic organisms, with fish being the most sensitive species. BPA can contaminate the environment directly or through the degradation of BPA-containing products, such as ocean-borne plastic waste.
